From 1860 to 1911 the British colony of Natal brought workers from India to cut cane on its sugar plantations. The first ship, the Truro, landed at Durban in November 1860. Over the next fifty years about 150,000 people came.

It was part of the wider system of Indian indenture that Britain set up after it ended slavery, which also sent workers to Mauritius, Fiji and the Caribbean. Workers signed five-year contracts, lived in barracks and faced harsh discipline. Many stayed when their terms ran out, as market gardeners, fishermen and workers. Traders, many from Gujarat, followed at their own cost.

White settlers soon pushed laws to limit Indian rights. That brought a young lawyer, Mohandas Gandhi, into politics after he arrived in 1893; he helped found the Natal Indian Congress in 1894. India stopped sending indentured workers to Natal in 1911. Their descendants form the largest Indian community in Africa, centred on Durban.
